title: Trade Induced Technical Change? The Impact of Chinese Imports on Innovation, IT and Productivity
research_question: Does increased import competition from low-wage countries, particularly China, cause faster technical change in firms in developed economies, both through innovation and technology adoption within surviving firms and through reallocation of activity across firms? How large are these effects on aggregate technological upgrading, employment, and firm survival?
data_description: The authors construct a firm- and plant-level panel covering twelve European countries (Austria, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Norway, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, and the UK) from 1996 to 2007. The base firm dataset is Bureau Van Dijk's Amadeus, providing accounting data on employment, capital, materials, wages, and sales, matched by name to the population of European Patent Office patent applications (with citation data). IT data at the establishment level come from Harte Hanks surveys (computers per worker and software adoption) for firms with 100+ employees. TFP is estimated for France, Italy, Spain, and Sweden using an Olley-Pakes/De Loecker procedure. Industry-level bilateral trade data at the six-digit product level come from UN Comtrade, concorded to four-digit US SIC industries; domestic production data come from Eurostat's Prodcom. Key variables include patents, citations, IT intensity, TFP, employment, exit, and Chinese import shares.
institutional_context: The setting is the dramatic rise of Chinese exports to developed economies after China's accession to the World Trade Organization in December 2001. Chinese imports to the EU and US grew from about 5.7% of total imports in 2000 to 12.4% by 2007, with sharp increases in industries such as toys, furniture, footwear, textiles, and apparel. A central institutional feature is the textile and clothing quota regime, originating in the 1950s and formalized as the Multi-Fiber Agreement in 1974, which restricted imports from developing countries. Following China's WTO entry, these quotas were phased out in 2002 and 2005 under the Agreement on Textiles and Clothing, generating roughly a 240% surge in Chinese imports in affected product categories. The pre-existing pattern of quota coverage varied substantially across narrowly defined products (e.g., 77% for cotton fabrics versus 2% for wool fabrics), reflecting historical bargaining decades earlier and providing variation in exposure to the post-2001 import shock.
